translate.output: Practicing calligraphy by copying the Thousand‑Character Classic is also acceptable, but it must be done consistently. If you copy one hundred characters each day without any interruption, then after several years you will inevitably become a calligrapher. Even when you are extremely busy, you must complete the day’s assignments; do not make up for yesterday’s delay today, nor postpone today’s work because of tomorrow’s obligations. Do not interrupt your reading lessons because of family matters, and likewise do not suspend them merely because an examination is near. Even on days when you are on the road, you may read at a shop; on the day of an examination, you may read even while proceeding to the venue.
translate.gold: For practising calligraphy, copying the Thousand Character Classic is fine too, but you must persevere. Copy a hundred characters from the model every day, absolutely without a break, and in a few years you will certainly have become a calligrapher. Even when you are extremely busy, you must still finish each day's lessons on that day. Do not, because of a delay yesterday, make the work up today; and do not, because you will be busy tomorrow, do the work today in advance. On no account interrupt your daily reading because there is business at home, nor interrupt it because the examinations are approaching. Even on a travelling day you can read once you reach the inn; on an examination day you can read once you come out of the hall.

translate.output: Then, is the very meaning of liberty ultimately impossible to practice by an individual? He asks: “What nonsense is this?” The freedom of a group is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot exist apart from a group; if the group does not protect its freedom, another group from outside will invade it, suppress it, seize it, and then what will be left of individual freedom? As a shallow scholar like myself, trying to explain it in a few brief words, how could I possibly know whether that is feasible? …Are there people in the world who truly love freedom? They must be careful not to poison freedom, for doing so would poison the whole world.
translate.gold: In that case, can freedom after all not be applied to the individual? I answer: nonsense, what talk is this? Collective freedom is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot survive on their own apart from the group. If the group does not protect its freedom, then other groups will come from outside to invade it, oppress it and plunder it, and then what will be left of the individual's freedom? For one of shallow learning like me to try to explain it in a few paltry words: how can I know that it will do? … Are there people in the world who love freedom? Let them take care not to poison freedom, and thereby poison the world.
translate.judge_note: The translation renders “然則” as “Then,” which introduces a sense of abruptness not present in the original; it is better understood as “In that case”.

translate.output: On the 23rd day of the fourth month of the 24th year of the Guangxu era, the Cabinet respectfully submits this edict: For several years, officials and workers, both Chinese and foreign, have been concerned with current affairs, largely advocating reform and self‑strengthening. Recently, several imperial edicts have been issued, such as opening special schools, reducing the militia, reforming the military examination system, and establishing primary and secondary schools; all have been examined repeatedly, planned thoroughly, and are now about to be put into effect. However, the prevailing atmosphere has not yet become widespread; opinions are divided, and some senior, concerned officials argue that the old regulations must be strictly adhered to and the new laws must be discarded. Many voices chatter, but their empty words are of no help. Consider the present situation: the state of affairs and national strength are as such; if we still rely on untrained soldiers, limited provisions, officials without real learning, craftsmen without good teachers, with strengths and weaknesses starkly contrasted, and the rich and poor at opposite extremes, can we truly hope to forge weapons and strike with strong armor and effective troops? …The Imperial University in the capital, being the model for all provinces, should especially be organized first, with the Minister of the Imperial Household Department, the Prime Minister of all state affairs, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs jointly and promptly discussing and reporting. …Let this circular edict be known. Respectfully.
translate.gold: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Secretariat received the following edict: For several years now, officials at court and in the provinces have studied current affairs, and most have advocated reform and self-strengthening. Recently edicts have been issued one after another: setting up a special examination, cutting surplus troops, reforming the military examinations, establishing schools of all levels. All were examined again and again and planned most thoroughly, and it has only just been proposed to put them into effect. But attitudes are not yet open, and opinions cannot agree. Some take cover behind experience and concern for the country, holding that the old institutions must be held fast and the new methods rejected. Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help. Let us ask: with the situation as it is today, and the state's strength as it is, if we still rely on untrained troops and limited funds, with scholars lacking practical learning and artisans lacking good teachers, the strong and the weak set side by side, the rich and the poor so far apart, can we really make clubs to beat strong armour and sharp weapons? … The Imperial University in the capital is to be an example to the provinces and above all should be set up first. Let the Grand Councillors and the princes and ministers of the Zongli Yamen deliberate on it jointly and report properly and quickly by memorial. … Let this be proclaimed to all. Respect this.

translate.output: The Director‑General of Internal Affairs, Cheng Dequan, submits this report. I respectfully maintain that safeguarding the people and defending the nation makes police work the keystone of administration; in selecting the worthy and appointing the capable, schools are especially a deep reservoir for cultivating talent. It is observed that Nanjing is currently the foremost exemplary district; all police matters there must first be genuinely improved, so that it may serve as a model for the other provinces. However, at the outset of the department’s establishment, funding is difficult; all expenditures are charitable, so frugality must be pursued. Accordingly, we shall convert the existing Jiangnan Higher Patrol Police Academy into the Ministry of Internal Affairs Police School, first enrolling 240 police trainees from the training institute, teaching them by subject as an immediate remedial measure. For the regular class of students, we will wait until sufficient funds are available, then hold examinations and provide instruction, in accordance with the Vice President’s aim of promoting the people’s welfare. We also immediately appoint the department’s Police Bureau Director Sun Runyu to concurrently serve as the school principal, hoping for swift implementation, so that it may benefit both public and private interests. All the reasons for establishing the police school should be formally documented and submitted for examination and implementation. It must be presented accordingly. According to the report, the western shore of Shaobo Lake has been barren for a long time; the representatives cannot bear to forgo its potential, and are arranging for its cultivation, which must not be delayed. However, the total area of that shore is a certain amount; it should be measured in mu, mapped, and first submitted to the department, so that it can be forwarded to the Yangzhou civil affairs chief for verification. We request that the representatives promptly comply, properly establish the share‑subscription regulations and procedures, and submit them together to the department. End of submission.
translate.gold: Cheng Dequan, Minister of the Interior, reports as follows. I humbly consider that for protecting the people and defending the state, police affairs are the key to administration; and for choosing the worthy and employing the able, schools are the place where talent is gathered. I note that Nanjing is now the capital, and all police matters must first be thoroughly reformed before it can serve as a model for the provinces. But this ministry has only just been founded and funds are difficult, so all measures should, it seems, be as economical as possible. I have therefore converted the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School into the Ministry of the Interior Police School. It will first recruit 240 police cadets for the training institute and teach them by subject, as an emergency measure. As for students of the regular course, as soon as definite funds have been raised, they will be admitted by examination and educated, so as to fulfil the President's intention of working to advance the people's happiness. I have also at once appointed Sun Runyu, head of this ministry's police bureau, as principal of the police school concurrently, in the hope of setting it up quickly, so that both public and private interests may benefit. As to the opening of the police school, it is proper to prepare this document and request you to examine it and put it into effect. This petition is necessary. According to your petition, the land on the west shore of Lake Shaobo has long lain waste, and you representatives cannot bear to leave its profit in the ground and plan to reclaim and cultivate it. This truly cannot be delayed. But you should measure in mu how much land there is on that shore, draw a map and first submit them to the ministry, so that we can pass them on with an order to the civil governor of Yangzhou to verify. You representatives are directed to comply at once, and also to draw up proper regulations and procedures for raising capital, and submit them to the ministry together. This is the ruling.
translate.judge_note: The translation renders '竊維' as 'I respectfully maintain' which, while conveying the sense of deference, loses the nuance of personal conviction and humility present in the original.

translate.output: Clause 1: The treaty concluded at Jiangning on the 24th day of the 7th month of the previous Ren‑yin year shall remain in force. The earlier Guangdong settlement concerning post‑war arrangements and the commercial regulations are now revised; having been incorporated into the new treaty, all former agreements are to be treated as null and void. Clause 50: Henceforth British documents shall all be written in English letters; for the time being they will continue to be transmitted in Chinese, but once China selects students to study and become proficient in English, Chinese transmission will no longer be required. From now on, whenever there is a dispute over wording, English shall be taken as the authoritative standard. In this treaty, the Chinese and English texts have been carefully compared and contain no errors, and this example shall be followed. Clause 51: Henceforth all official documents, whether inside or outside the capital, that refer to British officials or subjects shall not contain any foreign characters.
translate.gold: Article 1: The peace treaty concluded earlier at Jiangning on the 24th day of the 7th month of the renyin year remains in force. The supplementary treaty concluded in Guangdong and the trade regulations are now revised; since they have been incorporated into the new treaty, all the old treaties are null and void. Article 50: From now on, British communications shall all be written in English. For the time being they will still be accompanied by Chinese; as soon as China has selected and sent students to learn English and they are proficient in the language, Chinese will no longer be sent with them. From now on, whenever there is a dispute about wording, the English shall in all cases be taken as the correct meaning. The treaty now concluded, of which the Chinese and English texts have been carefully checked and found without error, is also subject to this rule. Article 51: From now on, in official documents of all kinds, whether in the capital or the provinces, the character 夷 may not, of course, be written in referring to British officials and subjects.
translate.judge_note: The translation of 第五十一款 incorrectly renders “不得提書夷字” as “shall not contain any foreign characters,” when the original means that the character 夷 itself should not be used.

Huxley was alone in a single room, in the south of England, with the mountains behind him and the fields before him; the scenes beyond the fence were vivid as if they were under the table.
He then imagined, two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar had arrived, what scenery this place might have had.
…Thus we know that the claim of unchangeability is certainly not a matter of heavenly destiny.
And the principle of the long‑standing formation of things lies precisely in continual change.
What we see now could be altered after twenty or thirty years, and likewise could be altered after twenty‑thousand or thirty‑thousand years.
By using past events to infer the future, we can speak of change as long, though we do not know its limit.
Nevertheless, while the heavenly order changes, there are things that remain unchanged within it.
What is the unchanging? It is called the Heavenly evolution.
Taking the Heavenly evolution as the substance, it has two functions: namely, competition among things, and selection by Heaven.
All things are subject to this, especially the living kinds.
The competition of things is the struggle of things to preserve themselves.
When a thing competes with other things, it may survive or perish, and the result belongs to Heaven's selection.
Heaven's selection is that, after the competition, a thing alone survives.
Thus its survival must have a reason; it must have obtained its place from Heaven's allotment, bringing forth its own ability, together with the time and place it encounters, and also the forces outside its immediate surroundings that cooperate or oppose it.
Only then can it avoid extinction and be sufficient to stand on its own.
Observing its effect, if a thing is especially favored and chosen by Heaven to survive, that is what we call Heaven's selection.
Heaven's selection occurs in nature; although it selects, it is not a conscious selector, just as competition among things has no deliberate contest, yet it is the ultimate contest of the world.
Spencer says, "Heaven's selection is the preservation of the most suitable."
Since things already struggle to survive, Heaven then, after their struggle, selects them; one competition, one selection, and the process of change arises.
translate.gold: Huxley is sitting alone in a room in the south of England, with hills behind and fields in front; the scenes beyond the railing are as clear as if they lay below his desk. He then imagines what this place looked like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar came. …… Hence we know that "unchanging" is by no means the way of heaven's course, and that the principle by which things endure and take shape lies, on the contrary, in ceaseless change. What we see before us may well be transformed in twenty or thirty years, or again in twenty or thirty thousand. It is only that, inferring the future from past events, change has far still to run, and we do not know where it will end. And yet, though heaven's course changes, something unchanging operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called evolution (天演). Evolution is the substance, and it has two functions: the struggle of things (物競) and the selection of heaven (天擇). This is so of all things, and most evident among living things. The struggle of things is things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing contends with thing after thing, it either survives or perishes, and the result comes down to the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is when things contend and one alone survives. Then there must be a reason for its survival: its endowment from heaven, the abilities it attains by itself, the time and place it meets with, and all the forces of things outside its body must have worked together and complemented one another. Only then does it alone escape perishing and become able to stand on its own. And looking at it from the result, it is as if this thing had been specially favoured by heaven and selected to survive: this is what is called the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is selection by nature: it selects, yet no one selects; just as the struggle of things seems to be no struggle, and is in truth the fiercest struggle in the world. Spencer said: "The selection of heaven is the preservation of the fittest." Since things struggle to survive, and heaven then selects among them after their struggle, with each struggle and each selection, change comes about.
translate.judge_note: The phrase 'vivid as if they were under the table' is a less accurate rendering of 'as clear as if they lay below his desk' than the reference translation, implying a more immediate and perhaps cluttered visual experience.

punctuate.output: 中國政治與文化之變革莫劇於殷周之際，殷周間之大變革自其表言之，不過一姓一家之興亡與都邑之移轉。自其裏言之，則舊制度廢而新制度興，舊文化廢而新文化興。又自其表言之，則古聖人之所以取天下及所以守之者，若無以異於後世之帝王。而自其裏言之，則其制度文物與其立制之本意乃出於萬世治安之大計，其心術與規摹迥非後世帝王所能夢見也。欲觀周之所以定天下，必自其制度始矣。周人制度之大異於商者，一曰立子立嫡之制，由是而生宗法及喪服之制，並由是而有封建子弟之制，君天子臣諸侯之制；二曰廟數之制；三曰同姓不婚之制。此數者皆周之所以綱紀天下，其旨則在納上下於道德，而合天子諸侯卿大夫士庶民以成一道德之團體。周公制作之本意實在於此，此非穿鑿附會之言也。茲篇所論皆有事實，爲之根據，試略述之。其條例則春秋左氏傳之說曰：「太子死有母弟則立之，無則立長。」年鈞擇賢義，鈞則卜。公羊家之說曰：「禮嫡夫人無子立右媵，右媵無子立左媵。」此二說中後說尤爲詳密，顧皆後儒充類之說。當立法之初未必窮其變，至此然所謂立子以貴不以長，立適以長不以賢者，乃傳子法之精髓。當時雖未必有此語，固已用此意矣。

translate.output:
The greatest political and cultural transformation in China occurred between the Shang and Zhou dynasties.
The great change between the Shang and Zhou, on its surface, was merely the rise and fall of a single clan and the relocation of the capital.
In substance, however, the old institutions were abolished and new ones established, and the old culture gave way to a new culture.
Moreover, on the outward level, the reasons ancient sages seized and maintained the world appear no different from those of later emperors.
Yet in depth, their institutions, rites, and the original purpose of establishing them were part of a grand plan for perpetual peace, a mindset and pattern far beyond what later monarchs could imagine.
To understand how the Zhou secured the world, one must begin with their institutions.
The Zhou system differed greatly from that of the Shang in three main ways: first, the establishment of the heir and the legitimate line, which gave rise to the clan hierarchy and mourning customs, as well as the feudal kinship system and the hierarchy of king, Son of Heaven, and vassal lords; second, the system of temple numbers (ancestral rites); third, the prohibition of marriage among people of the same surname.
These rules together formed the framework by which the Zhou ordered the world.
Their purpose was to bind ruler and subject within moral order, uniting the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, scholars, and common people into a single moral community.
This was the true intention behind the Duke of Zhou’s institutional reforms.
This is not a forced or speculative claim; the arguments in this essay are all grounded in facts, and I will outline them briefly.
For example, the regulations recorded in the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals state: “If the Crown Prince dies, the son of his mother’s younger brother is installed; if none exists, the eldest son is installed. The annual selection chooses the virtuous, and the rites determine divination.”
The Gongyang school explains: “In rites, if the legitimate wife has no son, the right concubine is installed; if the right concubine has no son, the left concubine is installed, …”
Of the two explanations, the latter is more detailed, but both are later Confucian classifications; at the time the laws were first enacted, they likely had not been developed to this extent.
Yet the principle “appoint a son based on merit rather than seniority, appoint a successor based on seniority rather than virtue” captures the essence of the hereditary rule; even if the exact phrase was not used at the time, the idea was already applied.
translate.gold: Of all the changes in China's government and culture, none is more drastic than that at the transition from Shang to Zhou. …… The great change between Shang and Zhou, seen from the surface, was no more than the rise and fall of one family and the moving of the capital; seen from within, old institutions fell and new institutions arose, old culture fell and new culture arose. Again, seen from the surface, the ways in which the ancient sages won the empire and kept it seem no different from those of later emperors; but seen from within, their institutions, their culture and their original intention in founding the institutions came in fact from a grand plan for order and peace for ten thousand generations, and their thinking and design were far beyond anything later emperors could dream of. If one wishes to see how the Zhou settled the empire, one must begin from its institutions. The Zhou institutions that differ greatly from the Shang are, first, the institution of succession by the son and by the son of the principal wife, from which arose the lineage system and the mourning system, and from which came the enfeoffment of sons and younger brothers and the system in which the Son of Heaven is lord and the feudal lords are subjects; second, the number of ancestral temples; third, the rule that those of the same surname do not marry. These are all the means by which the Zhou gave order to the empire. Their purpose was to bring high and low within morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, great officers, gentlemen and the common people into one moral community. The Duke of Zhou's original intention in making institutions truly lay here. These are not far-fetched or forced words: everything this essay argues has facts as its evidence. Let me set it out briefly. …… The rules are given in the account of the *Zuo Commentary*: "When the heir dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, he is made heir; if not, the eldest is made heir. If they are equal in age, the worthiest is chosen; if equal in merit, the matter is divined." The Gongyang school's account says: "By the rites, if the principal wife has no son, the son of the right secondary wife is made heir; if the right secondary wife has no son, the son of the left secondary wife is made heir; ……" Of these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed, but both are the extrapolations of later Confucians; when the rule was first laid down, its makers did not necessarily work out every case in this way. Yet what is called "a son is made heir by rank, not by age; the son of the principal wife is made heir by age, not by worth" is the essence of the rule of succession by sons; though these words may not have been said at the time, the idea was certainly already in use.
translate.judge_note: The translation's phrasing 'the heir and the legitimate line' obscures the original's emphasis on the principle of primogeniture through the mother's side, which is crucial to understanding the Zhou system.

punctuate.output: 弟向獲締交於季方，因得聞元方之賢思，一見爲快。昨於會城邂逅遇之，覺大兄之才華器宇更有勝於所聞者，正恨相見之晚，不期越宿分襟。又恨相違之速矣，別後初四日抵津門，初十日詣平舒，月未一圓，地經兩易，風塵僕僕，無非芸人之田，自憐亦堪自笑，比值同人歸里館中，惟我獨居，加以清磬紅魚，直是修行古剎，而西風黃葉洄溯時，殷雙鯉之頒定不，我棄尊體復元否？嫁務紛勞諸宜，珍攝因風寄意，不盡所懷，久不見碧梧翠竹之姿，每於月白風清，輒深神往，且以足下久不入，直爲疑近得阮昔侯札知駕遊山左種蓮楚邱者，已非一日青萍結綠，到處爭售所固然也，令弟才華意氣滿，謂嵆山獨鶴足以振采，雞羣何期牙琴一摧墓草已宿，令人感慨係之弟初客遼西，旋遊津淀，今春復有平舒之役，年年壓線依舊，幫傭良由村女蛾眉難爲時賞耳。

translate.output: I have recently become acquainted with Ji Fang, and through him have heard of Yuan Fang’s virtue, so I long to meet him for pleasure. Yesterday, in Huicheng, I chanced upon him and felt that my elder brother’s talent and bearing even surpass what I had heard. I truly regret that our meeting came so late, that it unexpectedly extended beyond a night’s parting, and I also lament how quickly we were separated again. After parting, I arrived at Jinmen on the fourth day and reached Pingshu on the tenth; the moon had not yet become full, and the region had already changed twice. The dusty wind and travel are nothing but the field of a wandering scholar; I feel both self‑pity and can laugh at myself. Compared with others who have returned home, I alone remain in the inn; with the clear chime and red fish, it feels like a secluded ancient monastery. Yet the western wind brings yellow leaves, the tide of time grows heavy, and the twin‑carp offering will certainly not abandon me. May your health be restored? The duties of marriage are hectic; you should take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts on the wind, unable to fully express what I feel. I have long not seen the green wutong and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I deeply long for them. Moreover, I wonder why you have not entered the proper path for so long. Recently I obtained a letter from Ruan Xihou, learning that he rides to the left of the mountain, planting lotus at Chu Qiu – a task that is not new. The green duckweed spreads everywhere for sale, as is natural. My younger brother’s talent and spirit, like a solitary crane on Ji Mountain, could stir a flock of chickens; yet unexpectedly a single strike of a stringed instrument and the grave grass has already grown, evoking lament. I first visited Liaoxi, then traveled around Jin and Dian. This spring there is again the campaign at Pingshu. Year after year the pressure remains, the servants are still the same, thanks to the village girl’s delicate eyebrows, which are hard to appreciate in time.
translate.gold: I, your younger brother, formerly had the good fortune to make friends with your younger brother, and so heard of your worth as the elder, and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday I met you by chance in the provincial capital, and felt that your talent and bearing surpassed even what I had heard. Just as I was regretting that we had not met sooner, we unexpectedly parted after a single night, and now I regret that we were separated so soon. After we parted, I reached Tianjin on the fourth and went to Pingshu on the tenth: in less than a month I have changed place twice. Travel-worn, I do nothing but weed other people's fields; I pity myself, and can also laugh at myself. Just now my colleagues have gone home, and I live alone in the office; add the clear chime and the red wooden fish, and it is just like an old temple for religious practice. With the west wind and the yellow leaves, I often long for you deeply; you will surely not abandon me, but will send me a letter. Have you recovered your health? With the wedding arrangements so many and tiring, please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by the wind, and cannot express all I feel. I have long not seen your bearing, like green parasol trees and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I long for you in spirit. I had wondered why you had not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learnt that you have travelled to Shandong and have long been serving in a secretariat at Chuqiu. Fine swords and fine jade are sought after everywhere: that is only to be expected. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I was sure, like Ji Shao, the lone crane, would shine among the flock of chickens. Who could have expected that Boya's zither would be broken, and that the grass on the grave is already a year old? It moves one to sorrow! I, your younger brother, first lived in Liaoxi, then soon moved to Tianjin and its lakes. This spring I have again taken up a post at Pingshu. Year after year I sew for others, still a hired hand: truly because a village girl's fine eyebrows are hard for the age to admire.
translate.judge_note: The translation renders '季方' as 'Ji Fang' and '元方' as 'Yuan Fang', which are transliterations rather than conveying the intended sense of 'younger brother' and 'elder brother' respectively, obscuring the familial relationship.
